new_statements.translation: Tonal realization rules generate these surface tonal units from underlying representations in which only two tonemes figure: high and low. [...] Koro can thus be described on the hypothesis of two underlying tonemes, high and low, which combine structurally to give tonal schemes very similar to those of the other Manding varieties. [...] The monosyllabic lexemes recorded all show either the tonal scheme H or the tonal scheme L(h) [...] Disyllabic lexemes are distributed among the three schemes HH, LH and LL(h).

new_statements.relation_note: Full tonal sketch: 2 tonemes, lexical tone classes, 11 ordered tone rules incl. H- and L-spreading, downstep, floating tones, definite = floating L+H; no mention of stress/accent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Koro (korokan) is a tone language: two underlying tonemes H and L; lexical tone schemes H / L(h) for monosyllables, HH / LH / LL(h) for disyllables, HHH/LHH/LLH for trisyllables, every lexeme must contain at least one final H (possibly floating); surface contours derive via tonal compactness, floating-H deletion, flattening of rising schemes, and Koro-specific rightward spreading of both H and L (rules R1-R11), yielding downstepped H and HL contour tones; the definite marker is a floating L+H. Nothing is said about word stress/accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not discussed (no stress statement at all)
new_statements.exceptions: non-lexeme units may have other schemes (B for pronoun à 'he/she', HBh for prohibitive kónè); automatic final raising/lowering of the last syllable of a like-tone sequence is noted (p. 83) and excluded from transcription; author stresses the corpus (one speaker, one session) is limited.
new_statements.identity_note: p. 81: 'Le korokan est un parler manding du Centre de la Côte d'Ivoire, localisé dans la partie Est du département de Mankono, avec comme centres relativement importants Tiéningboué et Bouandougou'; corpus recorded Dec 1983 at Wèdala, a village a few km from Tiéningboué (the same Koro test village, Wedala, used by Boone et al. 2000 for kfo). This is Koro/korokan of Tiéningboué = ISO kfo = koro1306, explicitly contrasted with the neighbouring koyaga of Mankono (koya1253). Not the Koro of Touba (korokakan) and not Nigerian Koro. | Title and p. 15: 'parler manding de la région de Tiéningboué'; 'le Korodugu (qui coïncide à peu de chose près avec l'arrondissement de Tiéningboué)'; distinguished from koyagakan of Mankono. = kfo / koro1306.

new_statements.quote: Il suffira d'indiquer ici que les monèmes du korokan se répartissent en monèmes de schème tonal haut (só "village", bésa "lézard") et monèmes de schème tonal descendant (sò "cheval", bèra "porc-épic", sisè "poule", tubabù "Européen"); dans ce cas, la place à laquelle est indiqué l'accent grave représente la façon dont le schème tonal descendant se réalise en fonction de la structure syllabique des monèmes.
new_statements.translation: It will suffice to indicate here that the monemes of Korokan divide into monemes with a high tonal scheme (só 'village', bésa 'lizard') and monemes with a descending tonal scheme (sò 'horse', bèra 'porcupine', sisè 'hen', tubabù 'European'); in the latter case the position of the grave accent [diacritic] shows how the descending scheme is realized according to the syllabic structure of the monemes.

new_statements.quote: The other Manding varieties mentioned in the present article are Baninko Bambara (Southern Mali), Kita Maninka (Western Mali), Korokan (Central Ivory Coast), Koyaga (Central Ivory Coast), Marka (Burkina-Faso), Maukakan (Western Ivory Coast), Niokolo Maninka (Eastern Senegal), and Xasonga (Western Mali). [...] 1.3.1. Phonology. As a rule, Manding languages have typologically unremarkable phoneme inventories including 5 to 7 vowels, plus nasality and/or length contrasts (depending on the individual varieties), and about 20 consonants. Manding languages are tonal languages with complex systems of combinatory rules responsible for frequent discrepancies between underlying tones and surface tones (see for example Creissels 2009: 19-39 on the tonal system of Kita Maninka).

In all instances, the tonal melody of a compound is dictated by that of W1, where compounds surface either [H#H] or [L#H]. 53 (14) Koro /krǒ / ‘Koro’ + /cɛ̌ / ‘man’ → [krò#cɛ́] ‘Koro man’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Koro (kfo) is treated as a Manding two-tone language (H/L lexical melodies such as /krǒ/, /tùbàbú/) whose compounds show the common Manding replacive ('Type 1') pattern: the compound's melody is dictated by the first member and the final member is raised to H, giving surface [H#H] or [L#H]; restated from Creissels 1987. tone_statements.citation: Konoshenko, Maria. 2014. Studying tonal complexity, with a special reference to Mande languages. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 563-586. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. hdl:10125/24616 [Koro: Table 2 p. 567, sec. 2.2.6 p. 572, sec. 3.1.2 p. 574, Table 3 p. 579]
tone_statements.quote: 3.1.2. KORO (< MANDING) Tonal contrasts: /H/ vs. /L/, also lexical floating (H) (3 pts.) Paradigmatic complexity score: 3 pts. Automatic rules: 1) L → eL / L__ ##; 2) H → eH / H__##; 3) L…L → H…H(L) / H__H, H__##, (H)__H, (H)__##; 4) L…L → H…HL / H__(H), (H)__(H); 5) H → L(H) / L__, (L)__; 6) (H)L → H(L); 7) downstep; 8) H(L) → HL __##; 9) downdrift; (9 pts.) Non-automatic rules: 1) tonal neutralization in compounds; 2) LHH → LLH for Noun + Numeral (2 pts.); Contextual floating tones: (L), (H) (2 pts.) Syntagmatic complexity score: 9+2+2=13 pts. Grammatical rules: no; morphological (LH) marking definite NPs (1 pt.)
tone_statements.locator: sec. 3.1.2 'KORO (< MANDING)', p. 574; also Table 'Number of level contrasts' p. 567 (Koro = 2 levels, source Creissels 1987) and sec. 2.2.6 p. 572 (Creissels 1987: 87 floating-(H) deletion rule excluded from the count)
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H and L (plus lexical floating H) with extensive automatic sandhi (spreading, final lowering, downstep, downdrift), replacive compound tone and a floating LH definite marker; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Konoshenko, Maria. 2014. Studying tonal complexity, with a special reference to Mande languages. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 563-586. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. hdl:10125/24616 [Koro: Table 2 p. 567, sec. 2.2.6 p. 572, sec. 3.1.2 p. 574, Table 3 p. 579]
sources.quote: 3.1.2. KORO (< MANDING) Tonal contrasts: /H/ vs. /L/, also lexical floating (H) (3 pts.) Paradigmatic complexity score: 3 pts. Automatic rules: 1) L → eL / L__ ##; 2) H → eH / H__##; 3) L…L → H…H(L) / H__H, H__##, (H)__H, (H)__##; 4) L…L → H…HL / H__(H), (H)__(H); 5) H → L(H) / L__, (L)__; 6) (H)L → H(L); 7) downstep; 8) H(L) → HL __##; 9) downdrift; (9 pts.) Non-automatic rules: 1) tonal neutralization in compounds; 2) LHH → LLH for Noun + Numeral (2 pts.); Contextual floating tones: (L), (H) (2 pts.) Syntagmatic complexity score: 9+2+2=13 pts. Grammatical rules: no; morphological (LH) marking definite NPs (1 pt.)
sources.locator: sec. 3.1.2 'KORO (< MANDING)', p. 574; also Table 'Number of level contrasts' p. 567 (Koro = 2 levels, source Creissels 1987) and sec. 2.2.6 p. 572 (Creissels 1987: 87 floating-(H) deletion rule excluded from the count)
sources.note: States Koro's tone system (after Creissels 1987): two level tones /H/ vs /L/ plus a lexical floating (H); nine automatic tone rules including final lowering, H-spreading, downstep and downdrift; non-automatic tonal neutralization in compounds and LHH -> LLH in Noun+Numeral; contextual floating (L) and (H); no grammatical tone proper, but a morphological floating (LH) marking definite NPs; Koro scores paradigmatic 3 / syntagmatic 13 / grammatical 1 in her complexity metric (2-level group with Bamana, Niokolo Maninka, Kakabe, Vai, Mende, Looma, Guinean Kpelle).
